To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the relative power of indigenous and colonial populations in the northern frontier of New Spain shifted radically, and often unpredictably, depending on the moment of encounter, and that this shifting balance was produced by the topography and ecology of the region.
the geography of the northern mountains of New Spain produced areas of refuge and vulnerability that affected the relative power enjoyed in the region by colonial and extra-colonal peoples.

the geography of northern New Spain produced areas of refuge and areas of vulnerability for both colonial settlers and extra-colonials, and that these areas shifted depending on the relative balance of power between the two groups.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interplay between topography and negotiation, in which the physical landscape of New Spain shaped the political landscape of colonial and indigenous life.
the interplay of topography, political power, and negotiation between colonial and non-colonial groups on the northern frontier of New Spain.
the interrelatedness of the colonial and extra-colonal spheres in northern Mexico and the United States.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the topography of New Spain's northern borderlands produced zones of refuge for both colonial and extra-colonal populations.

the geography of the frontier produced a dynamic and shifting balance of power, and that the history of conflict and negotiation on the northern frontier is best understood through a close examination of its topography.
the relative advantages of the two spheres of political life were contingent on the specificities of the local environment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the topographical and ecological features of northern Mexico produced zones of refuge and zones of violence that were often the same places.
we have found a complex topography of negotiation, in which the relative power of the colonial and the extra-colonal shifted depending on the moment of encounter and the location of the encounter.
the mountains of northern Mexico, and of New Spain, are a place in which diplomacy, violence, and refuge are inextricably intertwined.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the history of the northern frontier is not one of simple domination and subjugation of Indians, but a history of negotiation between two groups with shifting power relations, and a history of the creation of refuge zones by both parties.

the relative power enjoyed in any encounter between colonists and Indians was contingent on the particularities of place, and that these differences in power produced different kinds of political relations.
the relative power of the two sides in the frontier was not fixed but was a product of the specific topography and ecology of the place of encounter.
